items.title: Harness Engineering 2.0 is here!
items.summary:
Harness Engineering 2.0 is here!

We benchmark models all the time but the harness running the model can dramatically improve the result, cost, and execution time too.

And finally, devs just open-sourced Harness Arena, where you can test the same task across multiple harness and model combinations side by side.

You provide one task and then run it across several model x harness configs that you want to test.

Every config receives the same prompt, files, tools, skills, and evaluation checks. Harness Arena then returns:

- total cost
- execution time
- whether the task passed
- files and artifacts produced

If you want to try it yourself, it is implemented within the open-source HarnessRouter project.

Here's the repo: https://t.co/4y6zJShKSu

(don't forget to star it ⭐ )

HarnessRouter is a plug-and-play infrastructure layer that lets you run any harness under a single interface, like:

- Codex
- Hermes
- Claude code
- DeepSeek Harness
- System One, powered by Jev
- And 25 more agent harnesses

In Harness Arena, the cheapest run does not automatically win.

A config must complete the task correctly first. Cost and execution time are compared only among the configurations that pass.

Here's the result from one Harness Arena test:

- Hermes + GPT-5.2: 5/5 successful runs using 0.47 credits
- Claude Code + Opus 4.8: 3/5 successful runs using 223 credits

That is around 474x difference in credits, while the more expensive configuration also failed two runs.

You can keep the model fixed to measure how much the harness changes the result. Or vary both to find the best harness and model pairing for that task.

This helps answer practical questions such as:

- Should this task run on Codex or Claude?
- Can a cheaper config still pass every check?
- Which setup is best to handle this workload?

Once you find the best config, you can run future tasks through it using the same Unified Harness Protocol (UHP) interface for sessions, streaming, files, artifacts, cancellation, and failures.

So you are no longer choosing an agent stack based only on a model leaderboard.

Instead, you can benchmark the complete runtime on the task your product actually needs to solve.

To dive deeper, my co-founder wrote an article explaining why model routing is different from harness routing, how UHP works, and what supporting multiple agent runtimes involves.

It also covers the local setup, a working request, and how sessions and files move through the system.

items.title: 10 AI TOOLS THAT ARE TOO GOOD TO BE FREE, AND THE FINE PRINT THAT PAYS FOR THEM
items.summary:
10 AI TOOLS THAT ARE TOO GOOD TO BE FREE, AND THE FINE PRINT THAT PAYS FOR THEM

Ten AI tools give away, at no charge, capabilities that cost real money to run: frontier-class chat, a 1M-token-context API, a coding agent in your editor, Blackwell GPU time, studio-grade voice and full songs. I went through the official pricing pages, help centers and privacy terms of each one on November 10, 2026, and wrote down two things: exactly what the free tier gives you, and exactly what it takes back.

The second part is the exposé. The catch is almost always written down, just on a page most people never open: a terms section called "Unpaid Services", a FAQ line about thumbs-up feedback, a watermark footnote for three countries, a download cap of 7.

Every number comes from the company's own page unless marked unverified. X text can't hold logos, so each tool gets an emoji icon.

Each card is copyable. Value ★ is how much you get for $0. Catch ⚠ is how much you give up. Both ratings are mine.
The ten at a glance
 #  Icon  Tool               Category

 1  🧪    Google AI Studio   API / dev
 2  📓    NotebookLM         research
 3  💻    GitHub Copilot     coding
 4  💬    ChatGPT Free       chat
 5  ✍️    Claude Free        chat / docs
 6  🐋    DeepSeek           chat / API
 7  🦙    Ollama             local models
 8  🤗    Hugging Face       GPU demos
 9  🎙️    ElevenLabs         voice
10  🎵    Suno               music
🧪 Google AI Studio and the Gemini API free tier
┌─ 🧪 Google AI Studio / Gemini API
│ Free:  Gemini 3.8 Flash, 3.6 Flash,
│        3.5 Flash-Lite, 2.5 Pro, TTS,
│        Gemma 4. Free input + output.
│ Paid:  3.8 Flash $0.75 in / $3.75 out
│        per 1M tokens (to Dec 31)
│ Catch: free prompts can be read by
│        human reviewers
│ Score: ★★★★★  ⚠⚠⚠⚠
└──────────────────────────────────
What you get: Google's pricing page lists "Free of charge" input and output on Gemini 3.8 Flash, "our most intelligent Flash model, engineered for long-horizon software engineering, autonomous agents, and complex enterprise workflows." Also free: 3.6 Flash, 3.5 Flash-Lite, 2.5 Pro, the Live and TTS models, and Gemma 4.
Not free: Gemini 4 Argon, the Nano Banana image models, Omni Flash, and Search grounding. Free rate limits are shown per project in AI Studio, and "Specified rate limits are not guaranteed."
Paid equivalent: $0.75 per 1M input and $3.75 per 1M output through December 31, 2026, doubling on January 1, 2027. A month of 10M input and 2M output tokens is $15 by my arithmetic.
The catch: the row "Used to improve our products" says Yes for free and No for paid. The terms: "When you use Unpaid Services, including, for example, Google AI Studio and the unpaid quota on Gemini API, Google uses the content you submit to the Services and any generated responses to provide, improve, and develop Google products and services and machine learning technologies."
Then the line that matters: "To help with quality and improve our products, human reviewers may read, annotate, and process your API input and output." Google says it disconnects that data from your account first. 

Then, in bold: "Do not submit sensitive, confidential, or personal information to the Unpaid Services."
Two details: in the EEA, Switzerland and the UK, paid-tier data terms apply to free use too. And AI Studio counts as a "Paid Service" even at $0 if your account has a Cloud project with active billing.

Do this: prototype an agent on 3.8 Flash with public data, and move to a billed key before real customer data goes in.
📓 NotebookLM (now labeled Gemini Notebook)
┌─ 📓 NotebookLM / Gemini Notebook
│ Free:  100 notebooks, 50 sources
│        per notebook, custom chat,
│        analytics
│ Paid:  Plus 200 / 100, Pro 500 / 300
│ Catch: feedback opens the full chat
│        to review; visible watermark
│        in India, S. Korea, Vietnam
│ Score: ★★★★★  ⚠⚠
└──────────────────────────────────
What you get: the help page, now titled "Learn about Gemini Notebook's plans", lists 100 notebooks and 50 sources per notebook with no AI plan, plus source-grounded answers, reports, flashcards, slide decks, and audio and video overviews.
Paid equivalent: AI Plus gives 200 and 100, Pro 500 and 300. The plans page didn't render prices for my region, so no price is quoted.
The catch: the data policy is better than most. The help page says: "Your data is protected, and is not used to train Gemini Notebook unless you provide feedback." The exception is feedback: "When you share feedback to help us improve, we may review the full context of that interaction, including your queries, uploads, and the model's responses." One thumbs-down on a notebook of contracts can expose them.

Second catch: Pro and Ultra users can turn off the visible watermark on generated images and video, but "A visible watermark will be applied automatically if you reside in India, South Korea, or Vietnam."
Workspace accounts get a stronger promise: no human review "even when you provide thumbs up or down feedback."
Do this: load 50 primary sources on one topic, ask for a cited briefing, and never press feedback on private notebooks.
💻 GitHub Copilot Free
┌─ 💻 GitHub Copilot Free
│ Free:  2,000 inline suggestions/mo,
│        limited chat + agent mode,
│        MCP, CLI, entry-level models
│ Paid:  Pro $10/mo ($15 AI credits)
│ Catch: prompts, outputs and code
│        snippets may train models
│ Score: ★★★★   ⚠⚠⚠
└──────────────────────────────────
What you get: 2,000 inline suggestions a month, "Limited chat and agent usage", agent mode in VS Code, JetBrains, Xcode and others, MCP servers and the Copilot CLI. The FAQ: "GitHub Copilot Free users are limited to 2,000 completions and access to entry level models per month."
Missing: PR code review, file diff review, and assigning issues to the cloud coding agent.
Paid equivalent: Pro is $10 a month with $15 of AI Credits ($10 base plus $5 flex). Pro+ is $39.

The catch, for Free, Pro and Pro+ alike: "GitHub may use Copilot interaction data, including prompts (inputs), suggestions (outputs), and code snippets generated during Copilot sessions, to train and improve AI models."
The opt-out is at https://t.co/l6JkNi1MnW and "does not affect your access." Paying $10 does not opt you out.
Do this: turn training off, then use agent mode to write tests for an untested module. Read every diff.
💬 ChatGPT Free
┌─ 💬 ChatGPT Free
│ Free:  GPT-5.6 Luna, unlimited
│        everyday text chats, search,
│        uploads, images, 500 MB Library
│ Paid:  Go $8/mo (ads), Plus no ads
│ Catch: ads in some countries;
│        chats may train models;
│        feedback trains even after
│        opt-out
│ Score: ★★★★   ⚠⚠⚠⚠
└──────────────────────────────────
What you get: GPT-5.6 Luna, web search, uploads, data analysis, image creation and a 500 MB Library. The FAQ: "Free users have unlimited everyday text chats, subject to abuse-prevention safeguards."
Missing: scheduled tasks; memory with past chats is "Limited".
Paid equivalent: OpenAI priced Go at $8 a month in January 2026. Plus at $20 is from third-party coverage (unverified on OpenAI's page).

The catch, part one, is ads. OpenAI's ads FAQ: "Ads may appear for users on the Free and Go plans. Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu accounts will not have ads." Testing began February 9, 2026. OpenAI says ads "do not influence ChatGPT's answers." Free users can go "Ads-Free", with "fewer messages and no access to some tools like image generation or deep research."
Part two is training: "When you use our services for individuals (Free, Plus, Pro), we may use your content to train our models." The opt-out is Settings, Data controls, "Improve the model for everyone". The fine print: "if you submit feedback on a response, for example, by selecting thumbs up or thumbs down, we may use the entire conversation associated with that feedback to improve our models, even if you have opted out of model training."
Do this: use it to explain a new paper section by section, in a temporary chat if anything is sensitive.
✍️ Claude Free
┌─ ✍️ Claude Free
│ Free:  Sonnet + Haiku, web search,
│        code execution, files, memory,
│        connectors, 5 projects
│ Paid:  Pro $20/mo ($17 annual)
│ Catch: tight 5-hour + weekly caps;
│        training is opt-out; up to 5
│        years retention if allowed
│ Score: ★★★★   ⚠⚠⚠
└──────────────────────────────────
What you get: web search, code execution, file creation, memory, connectors, Artifacts, Claude Design, Slides and Docs, Incognito chats and up to 5 Projects, on Sonnet and Haiku.
Missing: Opus, Fable, Claude Code and Research. Usage is "Limited usage every 5 hours and every week", no number given.
Paid equivalent: Pro is $20 monthly or $17 on annual billing.
The catch: "Model training" is listed as "Opt-out" on every consumer plan. On retention: "If you allow us to use your chats or coding sessions to improve Claude, we may retain your data in a de-identified format for up to 5 years in our model training pipelines." Flagged chats are kept "for up to 2 years and trust and safety classification scores for up to 7 years."
Feedback stores "the entire related conversation" for up to 5 years. On the plus side, training excludes "raw content from connectors (e.g. Google Drive)", and Incognito chats "are not used to improve Claude, even if you have enabled Model Improvement."
Do this: put a style guide and reference docs in a free Project and draft inside it, after checking Privacy Settings.
🐋 DeepSeek
┌─ 🐋 DeepSeek
│ Free:  chat app and website
│        (no paid consumer tier seen)
│ API:   Flash $0.30 in / $1.20 out
│        per 1M peak, half off-peak,
│        1M context
│ Catch: data stored in China; inputs
│        used to train models
│ Score: ★★★★   ⚠⚠⚠⚠⚠
└──────────────────────────────────
What you get: free chat on web and app (my observation; I found no paid consumer plan, but no page stating "free" either). The API's deepseek-flash has 1M context, 384K max output, tool calls, vision, and OpenAI- and Anthropic-format endpoints.

Paid equivalent: $0.30 input and $1.20 output per 1M at peak, half off-peak. Peak is 01:00 to 04:00 and 06:00 to 10:00 UTC on weekdays (6:30 to 9:30 am and 11:30 am to 3:30 pm IST). My 10M/2M sample month: $5.40 peak, $2.70 off-peak.
The catch: the privacy policy (last updated February 10, 2026) names the controller as Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co., Ltd., registered in China. It says: "To provide you with our services, we directly collect, process and store your Personal Data in People's Republic of China." Input covers "prompt, uploaded files, photos, feedback, chat history." One stated use: "To improve and develop the Services and to train and improve our technology, such as our machine learning models and algorithms."

The policy also says DeepSeek may "obtain publicly available Personal Data via online sources to train our models", and I found no training opt-out in it.
Do this: run off-peak batch jobs on public data, like classifying filings. Keep client data out.
🦙 Ollama
┌─ 🦙 Ollama
│ Free:  run open models on your own
│        machine, no subscription
│ Paid:  Pro $20/mo ($60 cloud credits)
│ Catch: your hardware, your power
│        bill; 4,096-token default
│        context
│ Score: ★★★★   ⚠
└──────────────────────────────────
What you get: open-weight models on your own machine, "Run models locally. No subscription." The FAQ: "Ollama runs locally. We don't see your prompts or data when you run locally."
Paid equivalent: cloud Pro is $20 a month with $60 of credits. Cloud prompts are "never logged or trained on", running "primarily in the United States."

The catch: you pay in hardware and electricity, and big models need more memory than most laptops have. Plus a quiet default: "By default, Ollama uses a context window size of 4096 tokens." Long documents get cut unless you raise OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH.
This is the only tool here where the honest privacy answer is "nobody sees it", because local data never leaves your machine.
Do this: run a local model on documents you would never upload, like medical reports or salary sheets.
🤗 Hugging Face Spaces with ZeroGPU
┌─ 🤗 Hugging Face ZeroGPU Spaces
│ Free:  5 GPU min/day (2 logged out)
│        on RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell,
│        up to 96 GB VRAM; host 2 Spaces
│ Paid:  PRO $9/mo: 40 min/day,
│        10 Spaces
│ Catch: tiny daily quota, queues,
│        third-party apps
│ Score: ★★★★   ⚠⚠
└──────────────────────────────────
What you get: ZeroGPU on "Nvidia RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell", "up to 96 GB" VRAM, priced FREE. Daily quota: 2 minutes logged out, 5 minutes free, 40 for PRO. Verified accounts over 30 days old can host 2 ZeroGPU Spaces.
Paid equivalent: PRO is $9 a month. A dedicated RTX PRO 6000 Space is $2.75 an hour, so 5 minutes a day is about $6.90 a month by my arithmetic.

The catch: 5 minutes is a few generations, and quota "directly impacts priority" in the queue. A Space is also someone else's app: your upload goes to code its builder wrote. Check the maintainer first.
Still, anyone can try community demos, from image generation to speech recognition, on a data-center GPU with nothing installed.
Do this: compare three open speech or image models on one input before choosing what to run locally.
🎙️ ElevenLabs Free
┌─ 🎙️ ElevenLabs Free
│ Free:  10,000 credits/mo (~10 min
│        TTS), speech to text, sound
│        effects, voice design, music
│ Paid:  Starter $6/mo ($1 first month)
│ Catch: no commercial use; credit

└──────────────────────────────────
What you get: 10k credits a month across TTS, speech to text, sound effects, voice design and music, about 10 TTS minutes. TTS costs 1 credit per character; music 900 credits a minute.
Paid equivalent: Starter is $6 a month with 30k credits, a commercial license and Instant Voice Cloning.
The catch: "The free plan does not include a commercial license and cannot be used for any commercial purpose." Publishing non-commercially still costs you a credit line: "you must attribute it to ElevenLabs by including 'https://t.co/12X0XilDbz' or 'https://t.co/qFA8DqhFyH' in the title." Do this: make draft narration to check a script's pacing before the final recording.

│ Free:  50 credits/day (~10 songs),
│        v6-mini model, 4 in a shared
│        queue
│ Paid:  Pro ~$10/mo (unverified)

The catch-o-meter
How much you give up on the free tier, from my reading of each policy. One is barely anything. Five is serious.

Catch-o-meter  (⚠ = what you give up)

🦙 Ollama local   ⚠           data stays home
📓 NotebookLM     ⚠⚠          feedback = review
🤗 ZeroGPU        ⚠⚠          5 min/day, queue
💻 Copilot Free   ⚠⚠⚠         trains unless off
✍️ Claude Free    ⚠⚠⚠         opt-out, 5 yr
🎙️ ElevenLabs     ⚠⚠⚠         no commercial use
💬 ChatGPT Free   ⚠⚠⚠⚠        ads + training
🧪 AI Studio      ⚠⚠⚠⚠        human reviewers
🎵 Suno           ⚠⚠⚠⚠        7 downloads ever
🐋 DeepSeek app   ⚠⚠⚠⚠⚠       China storage,
                              no opt-out found
Side by side
Tool         Trains on   Human    Ads   $ use
             free data?  review?        OK?
──────────────────────────────────────────────
🧪 AI Studio  yes        yes      no    yes*
📓 Notebook   feedback   feedback no    n/a
💻 Copilot    opt-out    n/s      no    yes
💬 ChatGPT    opt-out    n/s      yes   yes*
✍️ Claude     opt-out    flagged  no    yes*
🐋 DeepSeek   yes        n/s      no    n/s
🦙 Ollama     no(local)  no       no    model
🤗 HF Spaces  per app    per app  no    per app
🎙️ 11Labs     n/s        n/s      no    no
🎵 Suno       n/s        n/s      no    no

n/s = not stated on the pages I checked
*   subject to that company's terms
model = depends on the model's license
Read the "$ use" column as "can I use the output commercially on the free plan". Only ElevenLabs and Suno say no outright. "Opt-out" means training happens unless you change a setting. "Feedback" means a thumbs button can send the whole conversation for review or training even when training is otherwise off; ChatGPT and Claude both have the same rule. For ElevenLabs and Suno I was looking at content rights, not training policy, so their training columns are not stated here rather than "no".
The decision flowchart
   Start: what will you put in it?
              │
     ┌────────┴────────┐
     ▼                 ▼
 private data      public or test
 (health, money,   data only
  clients, code)       │
     │                 ▼
     ▼            any free tier
 can it leave      on this list
 your machine?         │
   │       │           ▼
  no      yes     will you sell
   │       │      the output?
   ▼       ▼        │      │
 🦙 Ollama  paid    yes     no
  local    tier or   │      │
          business   ▼      ▼
          plan     paid   free is
                   plan   fine
Rules I now follow with free AI tiers
Rule 1. Check the training switch on day one. Copilot, ChatGPT and Claude all let you turn training off on free accounts. Copilot's switch is at https://t.co/l6JkNi1MnW. ChatGPT's is Settings, Data controls, "Improve the model for everyone". Claude's is in Privacy Settings.
Rule 2. Treat the thumbs buttons as a share button. In NotebookLM, ChatGPT and Claude, feedback can send the entire conversation onward, and in ChatGPT's case even after you opt out of training. Claude stores feedback conversations for up to 5 years.
Rule 3. Read the word "Unpaid". Google's API terms treat free usage as a separate category with human review. If your prompts contain anything you would not hand to a contractor, put a billing account on the project or use a different tool.
Rule 4. Check where the data lives. DeepSeek stores data in China. Ollama cloud runs primarily in the US. NotebookLM's watermark rule depends on your country. Location changes what laws apply to your data.
Rule 5. Rights follow the plan you were on when you made it. ElevenLabs and Suno both tie commercial rights to the plan active at creation time. Upgrading later does not clean up old free-plan output.
Rule 6. Watch for quiet changes. Suno moved to 7 lifetime downloads in September. Google renamed NotebookLM's help pages to Gemini Notebook. ChatGPT started ads in February. Limits and terms on free tiers move faster than paid ones, so recheck the page before you build a workflow on it.
What I could not verify
The dollar prices for Google AI Plus, Pro and Ultra did not render on Google's plans page for my region during this check, so the NotebookLM paid price is missing. Suno's Pro and Premier dollar prices did not render on https://t.co/MaoduTPQPu; the $10 and $30 figures come from third-party coverage. ChatGPT Plus at $20 comes from third-party coverage; OpenAI's own January post confirms Go at $8. I found no paid consumer subscription on DeepSeek's official pages, but I did not find a page that explicitly states the chat is free. Claude Free and Copilot Free do not publish numeric chat limits. Google's free-tier rate limits are shown per project in AI Studio, not on a public page. The value and catch ratings are my own judgment.
The pattern across all ten is simple to state. Free tiers are paid for with one of four currencies: your data for training, your attention for ads, your rights to the output, or a meter small enough that heavy users upgrade. Knowing which currency each tool charges lets you use all ten without giving away more than you meant to.

items.title: i used opus 5.5 to make an animated explainer about the sony walkman without any video model. it's a short cartoon where
items.summary:
i used opus 5.5 to make an animated explainer about the sony walkman without any video model. it's a short cartoon where a narrator called nori tells the story with real product photos. here's how

1. research
GPT pulled 9 facts on the walkman, each with the source sentence and the link. one failed, the line that the ipod alone killed the walkman, so it never went into the script.

2. content and script
opus wrote the script from the facts that passed. 8 short lines for nori, about 50 seconds, and every number on screen shows where it came from.

3. voice
cartesia read the 8 lines in one voice with an emotion set per line, and gave back the timing of every word. each line also picks nori's pose, like shock for the hook and thinking for the line after.

4. character art in GPT from different angles
GPT drew nori as an original character. one turnaround sheet with front, 3/4, side and back, then 7 poses: talk, shock, smug, sad, excited, thinking and facepalm. none of them has a mouth, on purpose. the mouth gets drawn in code from the voice timings, so it moves with each word. the png files are in the pics.

5. finding the real photos
every product on screen is a real photo. opus searched wikimedia commons and got about 30 candidates with their licences, kept 3, then cut them out or cropped them in code. the first render put the 1979 cassette walkman under the line about sony's download walkman, so we swapped in the player sony actually announced in 1999, the NW-MS7.

6. render and animate
opus turns the voice timings and a beat table into one html scene with the photos, quote cards, bars, word by word captions and nori switching poses. hyperframes renders that html to video at 30 fps in about a minute, then the voice goes on top of a quiet music bed. so the only pictures GPT made are nori's still pngs, and everything that moves in the video is html.

items.title: holy f*ck... the best AI agents don't have a better model. they have better notes
items.summary:
holy f*ck... the best AI agents don't have a better model. they have better notes

Stanford University just published the whole method for free in a paper called Agentic Context Engineering. your agent reviews every run, writes down each lesson and adds it to its notes. it never rewrites them, so nothing it learns is ever lost

same weights, zero fine-tuning. 38.6% → 64.2%, level with IBM's top production agent on Opus 5.5. fine-tuning for that jump costs $5,000-20,000. here it cost $0

it comes down to 4 agents:

→ worker: does the task and saves the full log
→ critic: reads the log and marks every mistake and every win
→ teacher: turns each one into a one-line lesson
→ librarian: files the lesson into CLAUDE.md. merges duplicates, never deletes a line

that's why asking your agent to "clean up" your CLAUDE.md is a mistake. every rewrite throws away lessons it already paid for

paste this into Claude Code:

"Run 4 agents on my last 10 sessions in ~/.claude/projects. Critic: mark every mistake and every win. Teacher: turn each one into a one-line lesson, what happened and what to do next time. Librarian: add only new lessons to my CLAUDE.md under ## Lessons, merge exact duplicates, never rewrite or delete an existing line. Worker: rerun 2 of the failed tasks with the new lessons and save the full log. Show me the diff and both results before saving"

run it after every big session. your agent gets smarter every time and it costs $0

本周 GitHub 金融 + AI 领域增长最快的 10 个开源项目

从 AI 量化交易、Claude Skills，到多 Agent 交易系统，这一周有不少值得关注的工具

其中 Kronos 一周新增 2,846 Stars，TradingAgents 新增 2,239 Stars

这里整理了完整榜单，建议收藏

01｜Kronos（+2,846 ★）
开源 K 线基础模型，基于 45+ 交易所的数据训练
过去 3 周里有 2 周登顶，这周再次回到第一
GitHub：https://t.co/Ba51vyZWVC

02｜TradingAgents（+2,239 ★）
多 Agent LLM 交易框架，目前累计 121K Stars
把交易流程拆成分析师、研究员、交易员和风控团队，让不同 Agents 在交易前进行讨论和决策
GitHub：https://t.co/S6yW7u8KHQ

03｜day-trader-skill（+2,061 ★）
专门为日内交易设计的 11 个 Claude Skills。
包括图表扫描、新闻追踪、止损规划，以及交易前的 session replay
默认使用模拟交易
GitHub：https://t.co/AmnKgx2i44

04｜last30days-skill（+824 ★）
一个很实用的 Agent Research Skill
可以跨 Reddit、X、YouTube、Hacker News 和 Polymarket 研究任意话题
并根据互动数据和真实资金参与情况，对结果进行排序
GitHub：https://t.co/G7rzLtXjvF

05｜tick-stock-panel（+638 ★）
面向中国 A 股市场的自托管量化工作台
通过 LLM 辅助编写交易策略，再进行回测和监控
GitHub：https://t.co/B91nRcuZI2

06｜Vibe-Trading（+540 ★）
来自 HKUDS 的个人 AI Trading Agent
通过聊天就能完成市场研究、策略回测和模拟交易，同时支持 MCP
GitHub：https://t.co/gCO99mgQER

07｜trader-skill（+508 ★）
和 day-trader-skill 来自同一作者
主要用于分析投资者 13F 持仓文件，以及追踪美国国会议员披露的交易
没有用户确认，不会自动下单
GitHub：https://t.co/BwJlXuhQmB

08｜Freqtrade（+388 ★）
比较成熟的开源 Crypto Trading Bot
内置 FreqAI 机器学习模块，支持策略回测、Telegram 控制和 dry-run 模拟交易
GitHub：https://t.co/nJWVbtfYRh

09｜daily_stock_analysis（+351 ★）
支持美股、A 股和港股等市场的 LLM 股票分析工具
可以每天自动生成分析报告，并通过 Telegram、Discord、Slack 或邮件推送
GitHub：https://t.co/QAoqu2gbe6

10｜QuantDinger（+256 ★）
本周新上榜的自托管 AI 量化平台
覆盖完整交易流程：
交易想法 → Python 策略 → 回测 → 模拟 / 实盘交易 → 监控
同时支持通过 MCP 接入 Agents
GitHub：https://t.co/MBb1OSQ3gU

这份榜单有一个值得关注的趋势：
AI 交易工具正在从单纯的行情分析，逐渐走向完整的自动化 workflow
过去需要自己组合数据接口、回测框架、交易执行和监控系统

现在越来越多开源项目，开始把这些环节整合起来
不过，GitHub Stars 增长不代表策略本身能稳定盈利

如果你正在研究 Claude Code、AI Agents 或自动化量化交易，这 10 个仓库值得收藏

items.title: The Gentle Singularity - Sam Altman
items.summary:
We are past the event horizon; the takeoff has started. Humanity is close to building digital superintelligence, and at least so far it’s much less weird than it seems like it should be.

Robots are not yet walking the streets, nor are most of us talking to AI all day. People still die of disease, we still can’t easily go to space, and there is a lot about the universe we don’t understand.

And yet, we have recently built systems that are smarter than people in many ways, and are able to significantly amplify the output of people using them. The least-likely part of the work is behind us; the scientific insights that got us to systems like GPT-4 and o3 were hard-won, but will take us very far.

AI will contribute to the world in many ways, but the gains to quality of life from AI driving faster scientific progress and increased productivity will be enormous; the future can be vastly better than the present. Scientific progress is the biggest driver of overall progress; it’s hugely exciting to think about how much more we could have.

In some big sense, ChatGPT is already more powerful than any human who has ever lived. Hundreds of millions of people rely on it every day and for increasingly important tasks; a small new capability can create a hugely positive impact; a small misalignment multiplied by hundreds of millions of people can cause a great deal of negative impact.

2025 has seen the arrival of agents that can do real cognitive work; writing computer code will never be the same. 2026 will likely see the arrival of systems that can figure out novel insights. 2027 may see the arrival of robots that can do tasks in the real world.

A lot more people will be able to create software, and art. But the world wants a lot more of both, and experts will probably still be much better than novices, as long as they embrace the new tools. Generally speaking, the ability for one person to get much more done in 2030 than they could in 2020 will be a striking change, and one many people will figure out how to benefit from.

In the most important ways, the 2030s may not be wildly different. People will still love their families, express their creativity, play games, and swim in lakes.

But in still-very-important-ways, the 2030s are likely going to be wildly different from any time that has come before. We do not know how far beyond human-level intelligence we can go, but we are about to find out.

In the 2030s, intelligence and energy—ideas, and the ability to make ideas happen—are going to become wildly abundant. These two have been the fundamental limiters on human progress for a long time; with abundant intelligence and energy (and good governance), we can theoretically have anything else.

Already we live with incredible digital intelligence, and after some initial shock, most of us are pretty used to it. Very quickly we go from being amazed that AI can generate a beautifully-written paragraph to wondering when it can generate a beautifully-written novel; or from being amazed that it can make live-saving medical diagnoses to wondering when it can develop the cures; or from being amazed it can create a small computer program to wondering when it can create an entire new company. This is how the singularity goes: wonders become routine, and then table stakes.

We already hear from scientists that they are two or three times more productive than they were before AI. Advanced AI is interesting for many reasons, but perhaps nothing is quite as significant as the fact that we can use it to do faster AI research. We may be able to discover new computing substrates, better algorithms, and who knows what else. If we can do a decade’s worth of research in a year, or a month, then the rate of progress will obviously be quite different.

Organizations can face enormous cloud bills when criminals steal access to their AI models. Google and Mandiant describe attackers running unauthorized inference and reselling compromised model access. One operation generated more than five hundred thousand requests in under eight hours. Their November second report says fraudulent charges exceeded one hundred thousand dollars in a day in individual incidents, with cumulative charges reaching one million dollars at some organizations before access was revoked. These are vendor-investigated cases, not a measure of how common the problem is.

Pregnant and postpartum people need reliable evidence that an AI health assistant actually helps. Researchers randomly assigned four hundred participants to Rosie, a generative AI chatbot providing maternal and infant health guidance, or monthly children’s books. Automated distress alerts were reviewed by a clinical social worker. At twelve months, the trial found no significant differences in anxiety or depression scores or several other health outcomes. Outcomes were self-reported in a defined population, so this does not establish that every AI health tool is ineffective.

Delirium can go undetected in hospitalized patients, making AI-assisted screening worth evaluating. A Mount Sinai model combines patient-record data with a language-processing score derived from clinical notes. Researchers evaluated it at a second hospital within the same health system without retraining. Confirmed detection rose after deployment, but the study establishes an association rather than better patient outcomes caused by AI. Its positive predictive value was about twenty-six percent, meaning many high-risk alerts were false positives; incomplete verification and the need for validation elsewhere also limit the findings.

Developers and users could face broader obligations over AI safety in China. Bloomberg reports that an official described accelerated legislation covering development through deployment, including data, computing power and algorithms. The reported framework would address risk management and disclosure of safety incidents and vulnerabilities. This remains a reported plan, with regulatory sandboxes and a transition period discussed. The report supplies neither enacted text nor a timetable.

Chinese companies renting overseas AI training capacity could face a new commercial constraint. The Financial Times, citing five people, reports that Nvidia verbally told cloud clients to sell at least fifty-one percent of services to non-Chinese entities. The reported requirement would apply globally to future contracts, rather than existing leases. Nvidia has not confirmed the percentage, and a written policy or enforcement method has not been verified; this is a reported company policy, not government regulation.

Security teams in restricted government cloud environments have another route to specialized AI testing tools. OpenAI describes Daybreak Red as access to models trained for authorized vulnerability research, exploit validation and security testing. The company says GPT-5.6 Cyber is available to approved customers in AWS GovCloud’s United States East region. Access requires both OpenAI approval and AWS provisioning; the announcement establishes availability rather than government adoption or independently measured security gains.

A customer receiving an AI answer may want proof that the provider used the promised model. Anthropic’s November second FlashProve research uses zero-knowledge proofs to check computation against committed model weights without revealing those weights. The proof concerns integer-model greedy token choices, not whether an answer is true. Anthropic released an open-source prototype and reports substantial computing overhead: roughly seventy to ninety-five times the GPU time used by its comparison system for equivalent prompt lengths. The fast executable verifier lacks a formal implementation guarantee, and no deployment plan has been announced.

Multilingual and disconnected AI could help services operating with sensitive data or limited connectivity. The government says EKA-1 supports all twenty-two scheduled Indian languages plus English. The smaller Dhir models are described as multilingual assistants for document-grounded automation and retrieval. Developers say they can operate offline and on mobile devices while keeping data local. India’s AI mission released EKA-1 and the two smaller Dhir models with subsidized national computing support. Those privacy and capability claims are not independent validation or evidence of deployment at scale.

Shoppers may eventually use an AI agent to buy products from other retailers without leaving Zalando. Its Extended initiative brings outside shops’ products into the platform, with Westwing as the first pilot partner. Zalando plans AI-agent checkout for Westwing products inside its app from 2027. That checkout is not generally available yet; the pilot and future purchasing capability are distinct stages.

Cyber weaknesses in essential services are the target of a planned British AI initiative. The National Cyber Security Centre says the National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability Centre will use AI tools to identify vulnerabilities across critical infrastructure and the wider economy. The Treasury announced seventy million pounds for the centre on October twenty-sixth, and the security agency has reiterated its AI purpose. The cited announcements give no concrete operating model or launch timing, so this is a plan rather than an operating service with demonstrated results.

Power constraints make more efficient AI inference a practical research priority. Lumai’s Iris servers perform AI computations using beams of light, targeting the compute-heavy stage that processes a model’s prompt. Britain’s Advanced Research and Invention Agency plans to evaluate the servers in its Scaling Inference Lab using real workloads in a commercial data centre. Claimed energy gains remain company claims pending that evaluation, rather than established savings.

AI in cars, cameras and robots can lose speed and energy moving data between processors and memory. Tohoku University and Aisin developed an AI chip with integrated nonvolatile memory, eliminating external working memory and storage for the described system. Their November second announcement reports AI-processing energy at one-fiftieth that of a conventional configuration and processing time about ten times shorter. Those are project-reported tests, distinct from operating-system startup improvements; commercial availability and independent replication remain unknown.

AI accelerators depend on memory components whose design affects speed and power efficiency. Maeil Business reports Samsung has orders for the entire output of its planned second Taylor factory, focused on high-bandwidth-memory base dies for AMD and Nvidia. The report places equipment installation from 2029 and mass production in 2030. Samsung has not confirmed the customer details, and Reuters attributes its account to Maeil, so these remain reported orders and future capacity rather than delivered chips.

Developers working with AI coding agents need to inspect changes and manage their code history. OpenAI says Codex already uses Pierre’s Trees and Diffs libraries for file navigation and code review. Pierre also makes the Git-based Code Storage service. OpenAI has announced a planned acquisition of Pierre and intends to integrate further features into Codex after closing. The companies remain separate pending customary conditions and regulatory approvals; Code Storage integration is planned, not already completed.

items.title: 🚀 Nature does not move in discrete jumps. Why should robot policies?
items.summary:
🚀 Nature does not move in discrete jumps. Why should robot policies?

Super excited to release ODE Policy — perhaps our most exciting breakthrough in my lab this year! 🤖🔥

Think about how humans reach for a cup. Our movements evolve continuously, governed by underlying dynamics. Yet, most robot policies — from Diffusion and Flow Matching to VLAs — learn to predict explicit actions.

What if robots learned how actions evolve, instead of predicting actions?

💡 That's ODE Policy for Embodied AI.

We use a neural Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) to learn continuous action dynamics, rather than directly generating actions.

One simple idea. Five types of robots. Multiple learning paradigms.

✅ Single-arm manipulation
✅ Dual-arm manipulation
✅ Dexterous hands
✅ Humanoid whole-body control
✅ Aerial robots

And it goes far beyond imitation learning:

⚡ VLA (π0.5): 96.0% vs. 75.5% success after one epoch.
🌍 4.5B World Action Model: 82.6% vs. 24.6% success, with ~4× faster action generation.
🏃 RL: More efficient humanoid whole-body motion learning.

For years, we've focused on scaling robot data, models, and compute.

But what if the next fundamental breakthrough comes from rethinking WHAT robots learn, rather than just HOW MUCH they learn?

Huge congratulations to Jindou Jia and our amazing team! 👏

PSA: there’s a fairly large phishing campaign targeting medium to large accounts across AI and robotics.

Got targeted twice today. Somewhat convincing accounts like @gregorymowens or @Conviasa will DM you with some “opportunity to collaborate”. These are legit accounts with high follower counts and sometimes counterpart LinkedIn accounts to fool any cross referencing you may do - sometimes they are impersonating a legitimate person.

They ignore any invite links you send and push theirs. It’s often a random invite link linke https://t.co/9CCixKSixU, or in @convisa case was a legit calendly link with a redirect URL form. 

Then they ask you to log in with your X accounts to steal credentials / oauth tokens.

In general be wary of people who ask for a meeting then ignore your booking links, and of course be wary of any booking page that asks you to sign up to X.

@elonmusk please ban these guys into oblivion

https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.
